<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par117" />is, however, somewhat rare in poetry, and even in prose it is not invariably necessary but is restricted to those cases in which the accusative of the object is more closely determined by being a proper name, or by having the article, or by a following determinate genitive (hence also by the suffixes), or in some other way (see below, c), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=1}} ''and she bare'' {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־קַ֫יִן|translate=Cain}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=1|hidebook=1}} ''God created'' {{GHGheb|text=אֵת הַשָּׁמַ֫יִם וְאֵת הָאָ֫רֶץ|translate=the heaven and the earth}} (but {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=4|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫רֶץ וְשָׁמַ֫יִם}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=25|hidebook=1}} ''and God made'' {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־חַיַּת הָאָ֫רֶץ|translate=the beast of the earth}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=24|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|b}}
Rem. 1. The rare occurrence of the {{GHGterm|nota accusativi}} in poetic style (e.g. it never occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=2–18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2}}, &c., though it is frequent in the late Psalms) may be explained from the fact that in this as in other respects (cf. {{GHGpar|2|q}}) poetry represents a somewhat more archaic stage of the language than prose. The need of some external means of indicating the accusative could only have been felt after the case-endings had become wholly extinct. Even then the {{GHGheb|text=את}} would probably have been used at first to indicate only an object placed ''before'' the verb (when it followed, it was already sufficiently characterized by its position as depending on the verb), or proper names.<ref>Thus, in Dt 33, {{GHGheb|text=את}} occurs only in verse 9 (twice, with an object preceding the verb), in Gn 49 in the blessing of Jacob only in verse 15 with a co-ordinate second object (consequently farther removed from the verb). Of the thirteen instances of {{GHGheb|text=את}} in the ''Mêša‛'' inscription, seven stand directly and four indirectly before proper names.</ref> Finally, however, the {{GHGterm|nota accusativi}} became so customary everywhere in prose, that even the pronominal object was expressed rather by {{GHGheb|text=את}} with suffixes than by verbal suffixes, even when none of the reasons mentioned under ''e'' can be assigned for it; cf. Giesebrecht in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1881, p. 258 ff., and the statistics of H. Petri, cited above at the head of § 58. Such examples as {{GHGheb|text=כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=22}} in the ''Priestly Code'', beside {{GHGheb|text=בְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר־צִוָּ֫הוּ יְהֹוָה}} 7:5 in the ''Jahvist'', are especially instructive.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|c}}
2. As accusatives determined in other ways, we have in the first place to consider the collectives introduced by {{GHGheb|text=כֹּל|translate=entirety}}, without a following article or determinate genitive, inasmuch as the meaning of {{GHGheb|text=כֹּל}} includes a determinative sense, cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=21}}, 30, 8:21, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=2|verse=34}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=25|verse=9}}. {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־כֹּל}} is used absolutely in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=3}}, cf. 39:23; similarly, {{GHGheb|text=מִי}} is determinate of itself, since it always denotes a person, hence {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־מִי|translate=quem?}} e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, &c., but never {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־מָה|translate=quid?}} So also the relative {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} in the sense of ''eum qui'' or ''quem'', &c., e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=3}}, or ''id quod'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=24}}, &c. Cf. also such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=2|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=24|verse=19}}, where {{GHGheb|text=אֵת אֲשֶׁר}} is equivalent to ''the circumstance, that'', &c.—Elsewhere {{GHGheb|text=אֵת}} stands before nouns which are determinate in sense, although the article is omitted, which according to {{GHGpar|126|h}} is very frequently the case in poetic or otherwise elevated style; thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=26|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=24|verse=14}}, 15, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=41|verse=7}} (to distinguish the object from the subject); 50:4 (with the first of two accusatives, also for the sake of clearness); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=13|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=43|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=13|verse=21}} (where the {{GHGheb|text=צַדִּיקִים}} are to be regarded as a distinct class); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=25}}<section end="par117" /><noinclude>
